Confirm
kon-FIRM
v.
From Latin confirmare, to make firm, from firmus, strong. Webster 1828: to make firm or more firm; to strengthen; to give new assurance of truth; to ratify. Scripture uses it of God ratifying His promise with an oath and of ministers strengthening the souls of disciples.

Biblical Definition

Confirm means to make firm, and Scripture applies it in three directions. Christ’s ministry confirms the promises: Jesus Christ was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made unto the fathers (Romans 15:8) — the incarnation is God keeping His word to Abraham and David, and Paul makes that the ground of Gentile hope in the same passage. God confirms His counsel with an oath: men verily swear by the greater: and an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife. Wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath (Hebrews 6:16-17). God swore by Himself because there was no greater, and Hebrews calls the result two immutable things — His promise and His oath — given so that believers might have a strong consolation. And ministers confirm the saints: Paul and Barnabas returned through the cities where they had just been stoned and driven out, confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22). Finally God confirms His people to the end: Who shall also confirm you unto the end, that ye may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 1:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines CONFIRM as to make firm or more firm; to add strength to; to establish; to give new assurance of truth or certainty; to fix more firmly in resolution; and, in law, to ratify or make valid.

expand to see more

CONFIRM, v.t. — To make firm, or more firm; to add strength to; to strengthen.

To fix more firmly; to settle or establish; as, to confirm a habit or an opinion.

To give new assurance of truth or certainty; to put past doubt; as, the news was confirmed.

To make firm or certain; to give new strength to, as an obligation; to ratify, as a covenant or a treaty.

From Latin con and firmus, strong — the root of firm, affirm, and infirmity.

Key Scripture

Romans 15:8 — "Now I say that Jesus Christ was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made unto the fathers:"

Hebrews 6:16 — "For men verily swear by the greater: and an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife."

Hebrews 6:17 — "Wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath:"

Acts 14:22 — "Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God."

1 Corinthians 1:8 — "Who shall also confirm you unto the end, that ye may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ."

Modern Corruption

Acts 14:22 shows what apostolic confirmation actually consisted of — the plain announcement that entry into the kingdom runs through much tribulation — which is the reverse of the encouragement most modern ministry offers.

expand to see more

Paul had just been stoned at Lystra and dragged out of the city for dead, and he went back through the same towns to strengthen the converts. The content of the strengthening is stated: exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God. That is not a caution appended to a cheerful message; it is the confirming word itself. Modern encouragement typically works by minimizing what lies ahead, and it fails at the first hard providence because the hearer concludes something has gone wrong. Telling a new convert the truth about the road is a kindness, and Paul evidently regarded it as the chief service he could render churches he might never see again.

Hebrews 6:17 gives the deeper ground, and it is one of the most remarkable statements in Scripture about God’s condescension. God’s bare word could not be made more certain by anything; He cannot lie. Yet willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, He swore by Himself — not because the promise needed reinforcing but because the heirs did. The oath adds nothing to God and everything to us, and the stated purpose is that we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us. That is the pastoral shape of the doctrine of immutability: God stooped to the manner of men who swear, so that trembling people might rest.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek bebaioo (G950), to make firm, to confirm, to establish; bebaiosis (G951), confirmation; episterizo (G1991), to strengthen further, at Acts 14:22.

expand to see more

Greek bebaioo (G950) — to make firm, establish, confirm; Romans 15:8, 1 Corinthians 1:8, Hebrews 2:3.

Greek bebaiosis (G951) — confirmation; a legal term for the guarantee of a title (Hebrews 6:16; Philippians 1:7).

Greek episterizo (G1991) — to strengthen upon, to confirm further; Acts 14:22, 15:32, 15:41.

Greek mesiteuo (G3315) — to interpose, to confirm by mediation; God… confirmed it by an oath (Hebrews 6:17).

Greek ametathetos (G276) — immutable, unchangeable; the immutability of his counsel in the same verse.

Usage

"To confirm the promises made unto the fathers (Romans 15:8) — the incarnation as God keeping His word."

"Confirmed it by an oath (Hebrews 6:17) — God stooping to the manner of men who swear."

"We must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22) — the content of apostolic strengthening."
